clue.text: Road signposted by Milne

parts.note: A. A. Milne wrote a comedy whose title names a road running from London to a Kent port; the clue asks for the port that labels it

explanation.surface: A road sign put up by the author of Winnie-the-Pooh.
explanation.walkthrough: A. A. Milne's 1921 play is The Dover Road; the town in its title is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The road in the title of Milne's play leads to this Channel port, so the place 'signposts' it.

clue.text: Provincial lady surprisingly defied all

indicators.note: a surprising result is an unexpected one, so these letters fall into an unexpected new order

explanation.surface: A woman from the provinces astonished everyone by defying them all.
explanation.walkthrough: E. M. Delafield wrote Diary of a Provincial Lady (1930), so the 'Provincial lady' is her signature book standing for its author.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist is best known for the Provincial Lady books, so the heroine's title stands for her author.

clue.text: Quintilian's "most learned (from the Var, Roman province)

indicators.note: the letters are taken out from the run of words that follows, ignoring the comma

explanation.surface: Quintilian praises a learned man who came from the Var region of a Roman province.
explanation.walkthrough: Quintilian called Marcus Terentius Varro the most learned of the Romans; the name sits across 'Var, Ro(man)'.
explanation.definitionFit: Quintilian's Institutio Oratoria names this Roman scholar as the most erudite of his countrymen.

clue.text: Updike protagonist going over railway to pets' home

indicators.note: in a down entry the first piece goes above, or over, the second

parts.note: Harry 'Rabbit' Angstrom is the hero of John Updike's Rabbit novels

explanation.surface: An Updike hero crosses a railway line to reach a home for animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A hutch or enclosure where tame bunnies are kept is a home for those pets.

clue.text: Unworried, like Oberon's imperial votaress

definitions.meaning: free of cares or romantic attachment
in A Midsummer Night's Dream Oberon describes the imperial votaress passing on 'in maiden meditation', untouched by love

explanation.surface: Someone untroubled, like the virgin queen Oberon describes in Shakespeare's play.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means without cares or attachments, and Shakespeare applies it to the untouched votaress.

clue.text: Impenetrable Verne character

parts.note: the hero of Around the World in Eighty Days is famously inscrutable, and his surname suggests a thick mist you cannot see through

explanation.surface: A Jules Verne hero whose nature nobody can fathom.
explanation.walkthrough: Phileas Fogg is coolly unreadable, and his name sounds like the weather that is literally impenetrable.
explanation.definitionFit: Phileas, Verne's imperturbable globe-trotter, has a surname that evokes murky weather one cannot see through.

clue.text: Into atonal composition, like the very process of writing music

definitions.text: like the very process of writing music

indicators.note: composing means putting together, so these letters are put together afresh in a new order

explanation.surface: A piece slipping into atonality, as is the whole business of writing music down.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing music means setting it down in symbols, which is relating to a written system of signs.

clue.text: Book associated with Max Beerbohm

parts.note: the 1890s quarterly to which Beerbohm contributed was named for a colour

explanation.surface: A volume linked with the Edwardian wit and caricaturist.
explanation.walkthrough: The Yellow Book (1894-97) was the decadent quarterly in which Max Beerbohm published early essays.
explanation.definitionFit: The colour named in the periodical's title, The Yellow Book, which Beerbohm wrote for.

clue.text: Crabbed country existence

parts.note: 'Crabbed' means written up by George Crabbe, the poet of village hardship, rather than sour-tempered

explanation.surface: A grumpy, sour-tempered life out in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: George Crabbe's poem The Village painted the countryside unsentimentally; 'Crabbed' looks like 'bad-tempered' but means 'as Crabbe wrote it'.
explanation.definitionFit: Life in the countryside, the subject of Crabbe's realistic verse on villagers.

clue.text: English vehicles for novelist Mary Ann can't in another form be hallowed

parts.note: vans are road vehicles

explanation.surface: English vehicles for a novelist named Mary Ann.
explanation.walkthrough: Mary Ann Evans wrote as George Eliot. The words after 'Mary Ann' repeat the end of 13-down's clue, a printing slip.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot's real name was Mary Ann, followed by this surname.

clue.text: Nobleman obtained by British Isles to take a part in King John

indicators.note: by means beside, so the word for obtained is placed next to the islands' letters

parts.note: a lord is a nobleman
BI is the abbreviation for British Isles
got means obtained

explanation.surface: A nobleman acquired by the British Isles to play a role in Shakespeare's history.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Bigot is one of the English nobles in Shakespeare's King John.
explanation.definitionFit: This English baron is a minor role in Shakespeare's history play King John.

clue.text: Monster in the Spanish style of tragedian

indicators.note: in tells us the monster goes inside the Spanish article

parts.note: la is 'the' in Spanish
an orc is a monster

explanation.surface: A monster done in the Spanish manner, as a tragic dramatist might write.
explanation.walkthrough: Federico García Lorca wrote the tragedies Blood Wedding and Yerma.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish poet-playwright wrote celebrated rural tragedies such as Blood Wedding.

clue.text: More company for bluestocking

parts.note: Hannah More published her tale about a fine gentleman in one volume alongside her poem The Bas Bleu, the bluestocking

explanation.surface: Extra companionship for a learned woman.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1786 Hannah More issued 'Florio' together with 'The Bas Bleu'; 'More' is the author, not 'extra', and 'bluestocking' translates the poem's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Hannah More's verse tale appeared in the same book as her bluestocking poem, keeping it company.

clue.text: Somehow select executive officer in defender of Thebes

indicators.note: in places the officer's letters inside the rearranged word
somehow means in some way or other, so these letters are arranged in some other way

parts.note: EO is the abbreviation for executive officer

explanation.surface: A chosen executive officer is somehow appointed to defend an ancient Greek city.
explanation.walkthrough: Eteocles, son of Oedipus, held Thebes against his brother Polynices in Aeschylus's Seven Against Thebes.
explanation.definitionFit: In Aeschylus's Seven Against Thebes, Oedipus's son commands the city's defence against the seven attackers.

clue.text: Across can't in another form be hallowed

indicators.note: putting the words in a different shape signals that their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Across, written differently, becomes something holy.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sacred or inviolable is hallowed, too holy to be touched.

clue.text: Count on him to find the dirty bits

definitions.text: Count on him to find the dirty bits

parts.words: Count on him to find the dirty bits
parts.note: rely on this censor to spot the smut, because his job is to cut it out of a text

explanation.surface: You can rely on him to sniff out the rude passages.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads like praise of a prurient reader; the man is a censor who removes offensive passages.
explanation.definitionFit: A censor who removes indecent passages from books must first locate the smut.

clue.text: Aristocratic, like Eliza Lynn Linton's Ms Kemball?

definitions.meaning: of noble birth, belonging to the upper class

definitions.text: like Eliza Lynn Linton's Ms Kemball?
definitions.meaning: Linton's 1874 novel takes its title from its heroine Patricia Kemball, so 'like Patricia' is the playful second sense

explanation.surface: A highborn manner, like the heroine of a Victorian novel by Eliza Lynn Linton.
explanation.walkthrough: Eliza Lynn Linton's novel is Patricia Kemball (1874); the question mark flags the jokey reading 'Patricia-like'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means noble or upper-class, and whimsically it can be read as 'in the manner of Patricia'.

clue.text: Amis's was Russian

parts.note: Kingsley Amis's 1992 novel title names a young woman from Russia

explanation.surface: A remark that Amis's subject came from Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: Kingsley Amis wrote The Russian Girl (1992).
explanation.definitionFit: Amis's novel The Russian Girl gives the noun that completes the title.

clue.text: Alcott's further notes on Lilliput?

parts.note: Louisa May Alcott's sequel to her famous novel about the March sisters could jokingly describe the tiny people Gulliver met

explanation.surface: Louisa May Alcott writes a follow-up account of Swift's land of tiny people.
explanation.walkthrough: Alcott's Little Men (1871) followed Little Women; Lilliput's inhabitants in Gulliver's Travels are literally tiny men.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcott's sequel to Little Women, whose title also describes Swift's diminutive Lilliputians.

clue.text: Lascivious goddess, like sailor, may be hot

parts.note: as means like
a tar is a sailor

indicators.note: may be signals that the following word could become something else, its letters reshuffled

explanation.surface: A lustful goddess, hot-blooded as any sailor might be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' rearranges HOT into OTH. Astaroth is a form of Astarte, the Phoenician goddess of fertility and sexual love.
explanation.definitionFit: Astarte, the Semitic fertility goddess, was associated with sexual love and appears under this name in Milton.

clue.text: Done by Keneally's daughter

parts.note: Thomas Keneally's novel A Dutiful Daughter suggests what such a daughter performs

explanation.surface: Something carried out by the novelist Keneally's girl.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Keneally wrote A Dutiful Daughter (1971); a dutiful daughter does what is required of her.
explanation.definitionFit: A dutiful daughter performs her obligation, the thing she is bound to do.

clue.text: Political pamphlet bodes heart failure

indicators.note: heart failure suggests breaking down, so the letters of these words break and re-form

explanation.surface: A political tract foretells a heart attack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heart failure' reads as a medical phrase, but 'failure' alone signals the anagram, and 'heart' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A large printed sheet bearing a political polemic, historically one side of paper.

clue.text: Spanish philosopher also gets say, anyhow

definitions.text: Spanish philosopher also gets say, anyhow

parts.words: Spanish philosopher also gets say, anyhow
parts.note: the philosopher's full name continues with Spanish y, meaning also, and a surname whose letters with that y are 'gets say' rearranged

explanation.surface: A Spanish thinker also gets a say in the matter, somehow.
explanation.walkthrough: José Ortega y Gasset: Spanish 'y' means 'and', and 'gets say' rearranges to Y GASSET, the rest of his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Ortega y Gasset was the Spanish philosopher of The Revolt of the Masses.

clue.text: Madame Eglantyne, who had an expensive habit

definitions.text: Madame Eglantyne, who had an expensive habit

parts.words: Madame Eglantyne, who had an expensive habit
parts.note: Chaucer's head of a nunnery is finely dressed, and a nun's dress is her habit, so the costly habit is clothing, not a vice

explanation.surface: A lady with a costly addiction.
explanation.walkthrough: Madame Eglantyne is Chaucer's Prioress in the Canterbury Tales; 'expensive habit' suggests drugs but means her elegant religious dress.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaucer's pilgrim nun, Madame Eglantyne, heads a convent of nuns under an abbess.

clue.text: Quiet cover for page to check

parts.note: P is piano, the musical direction for quiet
a roof covers a building

explanation.surface: A quiet covering for a page that needs checking.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial printing that is checked for errors before publication is a page to correct.

clue.text: Happily named tragic farrier

parts.note: Hopkins's dying blacksmith has the first name Felix, Latin for happy, which makes him happily named

explanation.surface: A blacksmith with a cheerful name meets a sad end.
explanation.walkthrough: Gerard Manley Hopkins's poem 'Felix Randal' mourns a dead farrier; Felix means 'happy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopkins's elegy names its blacksmith Felix, followed by this surname.

clue.text: Char a 20, perhaps

definitions.meaning: a char is a cleaning woman who comes in each day
20 across is a large-format newspaper, which is often published every day

explanation.surface: A cleaner, or perhaps one of 20 across.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Char' is British slang for a cleaning lady.
explanation.definitionFit: A cleaner who comes in each day, and a newspaper issued every day, such as a broadsheet.

clue.text: Necklace discovered in ancient Orcadian dig

indicators.note: the necklace's letters are uncovered inside the run of the following words

explanation.surface: A neck ornament was unearthed in an ancient dig on Orkney.
explanation.definitionFit: A Celtic neck ring of twisted metal is a type of necklace.

clue.text: Love to be Lawler's doll-fancier

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, written O
to live means to be, to exist

explanation.surface: Love is a passion of the doll collector in Lawler's play.
explanation.walkthrough: In Ray Lawler's Summer of the Seventeenth Doll, Olive keeps the kewpie dolls her lover brings each year.
explanation.definitionFit: In Lawler's play the barmaid treasures the annual gift of a kewpie doll from her cane-cutter lover.

clue.text: This coinage is not, said de Quincey, in revolutionary times, an infirmity of caprice

definitions.text: This coinage is not, said de Quincey, in revolutionary times, an infirmity of caprice

parts.words: This coinage is not, said de Quincey, in revolutionary times, an infirmity of caprice
parts.note: de Quincey defended the making of new words in times of upheaval, and a coinage here is a freshly minted word

explanation.surface: De Quincey argues that minting something new in revolutionary times is no mere whim.
explanation.walkthrough: De Quincey wrote that in revolutionary times new-word making 'is not an infirmity of caprice' but a need.
explanation.definitionFit: A coinage in language is a newly invented word or expression.

clue.text: Fox characteristic featured by Dahl

parts.note: Roald Dahl's children's book gives its fox the adjective as part of his title

explanation.surface: A trait of the fox, as Roald Dahl portrays it.
explanation.walkthrough: Roald Dahl wrote Fantastic Mr Fox (1970).
explanation.definitionFit: Dahl's Mr Fox is wonderful, the word in his book's title.

clue.text: Some of his audiences watched the clock, others got a surprise ()

definitions.text: Some of his audiences watched the clock, others got a surprise ()

parts.words: Some of his audiences watched the clock, others got a surprise
parts.note: the composer wrote one symphony nicknamed the Clock and another the Surprise, so his listeners hear both

explanation.surface: Some concertgoers were bored, others startled.
explanation.walkthrough: Haydn's Symphony No 101 is 'The Clock' and No 94 is 'The Surprise'; watching the clock sounds like boredom.
explanation.definitionFit: The Austrian composer wrote both the Clock and the Surprise symphonies.
